Research

With Damiano Caprioli and Luca Orusa

Galaxy cluster mergers drive shocks through hot, magnetized plasma. How efficiently do these shocks accelerate protons, and what does that imply for the gamma-ray signal we expect from clusters? I use three-dimensional hybrid particle-in-cell simulations with dHybridR to study this question. In the high-β, quasi-perpendicular regime, where thermal pressure dominates and the magnetic field is nearly perpendicular to the shock normal, weak shocks put less than 0.1% of the downstream proton energy into a high-energy population, while stronger shocks reach a few percent. The low efficiency at weak shocks helps explain why gamma rays from shock-accelerated protons have been difficult to detect in galaxy clusters.

Read the paper: Hybrid Simulations of Proton Acceleration at Oblique High-β Shocks

  • Hybrid particle-in-cell
  • dHybridR
  • Cosmic rays
  • Galaxy clusters

With Harley Katz

Little Red Dots are compact sources observed in the early universe. To learn about the gas around them, I extended the RASCAS Monte Carlo radiative transfer code to model Lyβ-pumped O I fluorescence and electron scattering. I use these simulations to compare how uniform gas, neutral shells, and moving clouds shape the O I λ8446 and Hα lines. Distinct gas configurations can reproduce the observed O I λ8446/Hα luminosity ratio. I’m now investigating whether the shapes and widths of the two lines can help distinguish between those configurations and constrain the nature of these sources.

  • Radiative transfer
  • RASCAS
  • Monte Carlo
  • Little Red Dots

With Anatoly Spitkovsky

Type I X-ray bursts begin when accreted fuel ignites on the surface of a neutron star and a thermonuclear flame spreads across it. I used a two-dimensional shallow-water model to study flame spreading on a rotating neutron star and test how the latitude of ignition changes the rise of the X-ray burst. By comparing synthetic light curves with observed bursts, I explored whether the first few seconds of a burst can reveal where the flame started.

  • Neutron stars
  • X-ray bursts
  • Shallow-water model
  • Light curves

About

I’m a PhD student in astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Chicago. I build and run simulations to study how particles gain energy in galaxy clusters, and what the light from some of the earliest galaxies can tell us about the gas around them. I’m especially interested in cosmic rays: how they are accelerated, and how they affect the gas in and around galaxies.

My work relies on high-performance computing, from three-dimensional particle-in-cell plasma simulations to Monte Carlo radiative transfer. Earlier, at Princeton, I studied thermonuclear flames on neutron stars.

I’m from Ukraine. Outside of research, I enjoy football, good coffee, and spending time outdoors. I also run the Ukrainian Student Society at UChicago.
